title: The State of EdTech in 2026: The Real Story Is Systems, Not Screens
author: Brewing Innovation
summary: This article synthesises CoSN's 2026 U.S. State of EdTech report — drawn from 607 survey responses from K-12 technology leaders — into a leadership framework arguing that the question of whether schools use technology is settled; the real question is whether they have the systems, staffing, training, and leadership to use it well. Cybersecurity remains the top priority for the eighth consecutive year, with nearly two-thirds of districts citing insufficient staffing and dedicated budget as primary barriers, now compounded by AI-enabled cyber threats and rising insurance costs. AI governance has matured dramatically in a single year: the share of districts with no generative AI guidelines dropped from 43% to 21%, with most districts moving toward use-case-specific strategies rather than blanket bans or uncritical adoption. The most significant operational gap runs along a precise fault line: while districts generally report adequate technical infrastructure support (networks, applications, maintenance), 58% are understaffed specifically for technology used in teaching and learning — the coaching and professional learning layer that determines whether tools improve instruction. The article closes with five leadership moves for district and school leaders: treat cybersecurity as a cabinet-level priority, build AI guidance as a living system beyond the policy document, invest in instructional coaching rather than just technical support, communicate purposefully with families about screen-time nuance, and tighten procurement around privacy, accessibility, interoperability, and evidence of effectiveness.
points: The share of districts with no generative AI guidelines dropped from 43% to 21% in a single year, signalling rapid governance maturation — but the goal should not be a finished policy document but a living system of guidance, modelling, professional learning, and reflection.

The staffing gap splits along a critical fault line: districts are broadly adequate for technical infrastructure support but 58% are understaffed for instructional technology support — the coaching that determines whether tools actually improve teaching rather than becoming another burden.

Community concern is highest around personal device use, not educational technology used for teaching and learning — a distinction that should shape how leaders frame the screen-time conversation with families and avoid flattening meaningful differences.

Home connectivity and device access gaps persist even as 1:1 programs proliferate, creating the risk that AI tutoring and personalised learning tools become a new privilege gap if districts lack complete data about which students can connect reliably outside school.

Only 11% of districts formally embed accessibility compliance in procurement policies, and 24% have no established interoperability assessment process — procurement gaps that create privacy risk, coherence failures, and marginalised learner access problems downstream.
quotes: EdTech in 2026 is not about whether schools use technology. That debate is over. The real question is whether schools have the systems, staffing, training, and leadership to use it well.

Nearly two-thirds of districts identify insufficient cybersecurity staffing and lack of a dedicated budget as top barriers. Add rising cyber insurance costs and AI-enabled cyber threats, and the challenge becomes even more complex.

The goal is not to create the perfect AI policy and call the work done. The goal is to build a living system of guidance, modeling, professional learning, and reflection. AI changes too quickly for a policy binder to be the whole strategy.
For many teachers and administrators, AI's first real value is not some futuristic classroom redesign. It is getting time back.
Without that support, technology becomes one more thing on the plate. With that support, it can become a lever for better teaching and learning.
A 1:1 program does not automatically create equity. A device does not guarantee access. A login does not guarantee opportunity.

Technology is not the strategy. The system is the strategy. The districts that thrive will not be the ones with the most tools. They will be the ones with the clearest purpose, strongest guardrails, best communication, and deepest investment in people.
